title: Life in the palace
hook: music, gardens, the king's fear that his son will leave (Buddhacarita 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asita's tears, an old sage weeping because he won't hear the child teach. Your line: born too early. And today is day seven hundred.

In the evenings, music drifts down from the upper rooms of the palace. Women play and sing. The rooms open onto gardens. Down below, the poem says, the whole land seems to flourish after the boy is born. Everything a young prince could want is brought upstairs to him. And the man who arranged all of it is afraid. It's the king. He keeps hearing an old sage's voice telling him his son will leave the kingdom. So he has decided what to do about it.
screen: `MUSIC FROM THE TOP FLOOR.` → `A KINGDOM DOING WELL.` → `A KING WHO IS AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Year one told the palace years from the prince's side, in his own later words: three palaces, one for each season, and a life of great comfort. The poem moves the camera. It shows the palace through his father. First, the plan. The poem says plainly why the king fills the prince's days with pleasure: he remembers what Asita foretold, and wants the boy so delighted with home that he never thinks of the forest. The music isn't only a gift. It's a strategy. Second, the details. The prince grows up in the upper rooms, among music and dancing, while out in the kingdom the king rules well and does good works, as if he could hold everything steady by being good enough. Third, the family. The king arranges a marriage, to Yashodhara, and in time a son is born, Rahula. The king is glad: a grandson is one more thread holding the prince to home. And fourth, the fear underneath. Nothing in the palace is cruel. Every gift is real, and every gift is also a wall. The king isn't a villain; he's a father trying to write his son's story for him. Some listeners will know that father. Some have been him. The poem doesn't mock him. It shows how hard he's holding on, and quietly suggests the holding won't be enough.
screen: `THE PALACE, SEEN THROUGH THE FATHER.` · `PLEASURE AS A PLAN.` · `A WIFE, A SON, ONE MORE THREAD.` · `EVERY GIFT IS ALSO A WALL.` · then, large: `A FATHER'S FEAR.`

segments.voice: Look gently around the life you have for one thing you've been protected from: a hard truth a parent kept from you when you were small, trouble your neighborhood keeps out of sight, a phone that shows you only what you already like. Don't judge whoever built the wall, and don't tear it down in your head; just see it, and notice whether it came from love, or fear, or both.
Life in the palace. Music, gardens, a marriage and a son, all arranged by a king who fears his son will leave. Today's word.
Your line: a father's fear. Tomorrow, something finally gets through the walls. That's day seven hundred.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on the palace years when speaking about comfort, attachment and family love, and the story appears in temple murals and in children's classes in Buddhist communities.

fill his life with every pleasure so he never wants to leave.

chat.says: Why did the Buddha's father fill the palace with music and pleasure?
options: He feared the prophecy, and hoped his son would never want to leave.
He wanted to train his son in the arts a king must know.
He was celebrating his son's marriage and a new grandson.
chat.meaning: Remembering Asita's words, the king wanted the boy so delighted with home that he'd never think of the forest.

Asita.meaning: the old sage who foretold the prince would leave

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 not on the validator list).
